blocks.text: A heart transplant recipient has a resting pulse of about 100 beats per minute, faster than most healthy adults, and when he starts to walk briskly his pulse barely changes at first, yet his stroke volume climbs and he copes. The new heart has been cut off from its nerves, so we can see what the heart does by itself and what the autonomic nerves add. Cardiac output is set by two things, heart rate and stroke volume, and each has its own controls.

blocks.markdown:
Cardiac output (CO) is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute. It is the product of **heart rate (HR)**, in beats per minute, and **stroke volume (SV)**, the volume ejected per beat in mL. At rest, an adult with HR 72 beats per minute and SV 70 mL has a cardiac output of about 5 L/min. Both ventricles must pump the same output over time, because they are in series; a persistent mismatch would flood the lungs or starve the body.

Stroke volume is set by three factors. **Preload** is the stretch of the ventricular wall at the end of filling, determined by end-diastolic volume (EDV) and so by venous return. **Afterload** is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject, mainly aortic pressure. **Contractility** is the force of contraction at a given preload and afterload, which changes with the sympathetic nervous system.

blocks.caption: Cardiac output. HR in beats per minute, SV in mL per beat, so CO in mL/min (divide by 1000 for L/min).

blocks.title: Calculating cardiac output
blocks.prompt: A resting adult has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. Calculate cardiac output in L/min.

steps.text: Multiply rate by stroke volume: 72 x 70 = 5040 mL/min.
Interpretation: this is within the typical resting range of roughly 4 to 6 L/min.

blocks.title: The Frank-Starling relationship
blocks.text: The Frank-Starling relationship (the Frank-Starling law of the heart) states that, within physiological limits, the greater the end-diastolic volume (preload), the greater the stroke volume. A greater filling stretches the cardiac sarcomeres towards their optimal overlap and increases the sensitivity of the contractile proteins to calcium, so the ventricle contracts more forcefully on the next beat.

blocks.markdown: **Significance of the Frank-Starling relationship.** The relationship is intrinsic to heart muscle, so it needs no nerves or hormones, as the transplant recipient shows. It matches the output of the two ventricles beat by beat: if the right ventricle momentarily pumps more, the left ventricle receives more filling and automatically ejects more. It also lets the heart increase stroke volume within a single beat when venous return rises, for example when a person lies down or begins to move. The relationship has an ascending limb in healthy hearts operating at physiological volumes; very large overstretching in a diseased heart flattens or reduces the response.

blocks.title: A denervated heart responds to a rise in venous return
blocks.prompt: A transplant recipient (no autonomic nerve supply) has an intrinsic heart rate of 100 beats per minute and a resting stroke volume of 55 mL. During the first minute of activity, heart rate stays about 100 but venous return increases so that EDV rises and stroke volume reaches 70 mL. Calculate the change in cardiac output and say why it occurred.

steps.text: Resting cardiac output: 100 x 55 = 5500 mL/min = 5.5 L/min.
Cardiac output at the start of activity: 100 x 70 = 7000 mL/min = 7.0 L/min.
Change: 7.0 - 5.5 = 1.5 L/min, an increase of about 27 percent.

The rise came entirely from stroke volume: more venous return raised EDV, stretching the myocardium so each beat ejected more (Frank-Starling). No nerve signal was needed. Heart rate would rise later, only slowly, in response to circulating adrenaline.

blocks.answer: Cardiac output rises by 1.5 L/min (5.5 to 7.0 L/min) through the Frank-Starling mechanism alone.

blocks.markdown:
**Autonomic control.** The SA node receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves; the ventricles receive mainly sympathetic nerves.

**Sympathetic stimulation.** Noradrenaline released by the cardiac sympathetic nerves (and circulating adrenaline) acts on beta-1 adrenoceptors, raising cyclic AMP and protein kinase A activity. In the SA node this steepens the pacemaker potential (greater funny current and Ca2+ current), so heart rate rises (a positive chronotropic effect). In the atrioventricular node it speeds conduction. In the myocardium, phosphorylation of L-type Ca2+ channels and of sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins increases Ca2+ entry and storage, so contraction is stronger (positive inotropic effect) and relaxation faster, which shortens systole and preserves filling time at higher rates.

**Parasympathetic stimulation.** Acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve acts on M2 muscarinic receptors at the SA and AV nodes. It lowers cyclic AMP and opens K+ channels, so nodal cells hyperpolarise and the pacemaker potential is flatter: heart rate falls (negative chronotropic effect) and AV conduction slows. The vagus has little direct influence on ventricular contractility because the ventricles have sparse parasympathetic innervation. At rest vagal tone dominates, which is why the resting rate is lower than the intrinsic SA node rate of about 100 beats per minute.

blocks.caption: Determinants of cardiac output and how each acts.
rows: M2 receptors, K+ channel opening, lower cAMP
Frank-Starling: sarcomere stretch and Ca2+ sensitivity
More Ca2+ available to contractile proteins

items: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume; each ventricle pumps the same long-term output.
Preload (EDV) governs SV through the Frank-Starling relationship, independently of nerves.
Sympathetic nerves raise HR and contractility through beta-1 receptors and cAMP.
The vagus lowers HR and slows AV conduction through M2 receptors, with little direct effect on ventricular contractility.
Resting heart rate is set by vagal tone braking the intrinsic SA rate of about 100 beats per minute.

blocks.title: Two kinds of stroke volume control
blocks.text: Stroke volume can change because the ventricle fills more (a move along the Frank-Starling curve, intrinsic) or because contractility changes (a shift of the curve, set by sympathetic stimulation). Keep these separate: preload changes the position on a curve, whereas contractility changes the curve itself.

blocks.title: Do not give the vagus a ventricular role
blocks.text: Acetylcholine strongly slows the SA node and the AV node, but it has only a small direct effect on ventricular force. The ventricular inotropic control is sympathetic, and the parasympathetic action is mainly chronotropic.

points: CO = HR x SV, with SV determined by preload, afterload and contractility.
The Frank-Starling relationship states that greater end-diastolic stretch gives a greater stroke volume, matching ventricular outputs and adjusting to changes in venous return.
Sympathetic stimulation raises heart rate and contractility via beta-1 receptors; parasympathetic stimulation slows the SA and AV nodes via M2 receptors.
A denervated heart still raises stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism.

questions.stem: According to the Frank-Starling relationship, what happens when end-diastolic volume increases within physiological limits?

options.text: Stroke volume increases because the stretched myocardium contracts more forcefully
Stroke volume decreases because the ventricle is overfilled
Heart rate increases through vagal withdrawal
Stroke volume is unchanged because it depends only on nerve activity

questions.correctOptionText: Stroke volume increases because the stretched myocardium contracts more forcefully

distractorRationale.a: Correct: greater preload stretches sarcomeres and increases Ca2+ sensitivity, so the next contraction is stronger.
distractorRationale.b: Within physiological limits the response is an increase; a fall occurs only in marked overstretching of a diseased ventricle.
distractorRationale.c: The relationship concerns stroke volume, not a nerve-mediated change in heart rate.
distractorRationale.d: The mechanism is intrinsic to the muscle and does not need nerve activity.

questions.explanation: The Frank-Starling relationship links filling to ejection: more end-diastolic stretch produces a stronger contraction and a larger stroke volume. It operates without nerves or hormones, so it adjusts output immediately to changes in venous return.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the physiological significance of the Frank-Starling relationship?

options.text: It matches the outputs of the right and left ventricles and adjusts stroke volume to changes in venous return
It sets the resting heart rate through vagal tone
It raises contractility via beta-1 receptors during stress
It determines afterload through arteriolar tone

questions.correctOptionText: It matches the outputs of the right and left ventricles and adjusts stroke volume to changes in venous return

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the intrinsic response balances the two ventricles and adapts stroke volume beat by beat.
distractorRationale.b: Resting heart rate is set by vagal tone acting on the SA node, not by the Frank-Starling relationship.
distractorRationale.c: Beta-1 mediated contractility is a sympathetic mechanism that shifts the curve, separate from the relationship itself.
distractorRationale.d: Afterload depends on arterial pressure and vascular tone.

questions.explanation: Because the ventricles are in series, any mismatch must be corrected automatically. The Frank-Starling relationship does this: a greater return to a ventricle gives a larger filling and larger ejection. It also adapts output to changes in venous return, without nervous input.

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate by which cellular effect in sinoatrial node cells?

options.text: Beta-1 receptor activation raises cAMP and steepens the pacemaker potential
M2 receptor activation opens K+ channels and hyperpolarises the cell
Reduced cAMP in the nodal cell

questions.correctOptionText: Beta-1 receptor activation raises cAMP and steepens the pacemaker potential

distractorRationale.a: Correct: higher cAMP increases the funny and calcium currents so threshold is reached sooner.
distractorRationale.b: This describes the parasympathetic action, which slows the heart.
distractorRationale.c: Blocking calcium channels would slow nodal depolarisation.
distractorRationale.d: Reduced cAMP is the vagal effect and would slow the pacemaker.

questions.explanation: Noradrenaline binds beta-1 receptors, raising cAMP and PKA activity, which increases the currents that drive phase 4 depolarisation. The pacemaker potential is steeper, threshold is reached sooner and heart rate rises.

questions.stem: Vagal stimulation of the heart produces which of the following?

options.text: Slowed sinoatrial firing and atrioventricular conduction, with little direct effect on ventricular contractility
Faster sinoatrial firing and greatly increased ventricular contractility
Slowed sinoatrial firing and a large fall in ventricular contractility
Faster atrioventricular conduction through beta-1 receptors

questions.correctOptionText: Slowed sinoatrial firing and atrioventricular conduction, with little direct effect on ventricular contractility

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors at the SA and AV nodes, and the ventricles have sparse vagal innervation.
distractorRationale.c: The ventricular effect of vagal stimulation is small, not large.
distractorRationale.d: Faster AV conduction is a sympathetic effect.

questions.explanation: Acetylcholine from the vagus acts on M2 receptors to hyperpolarise nodal cells and lower cAMP, slowing the SA node and AV conduction. The ventricular myocardium has little parasympathetic innervation, so there is little direct effect on contractility.

questions.stem: True or false: Parasympathetic stimulation markedly increases ventricular contractility.
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic effect is mainly on the nodes, where it slows the heart rate and AV conduction. Increased contractility is a sympathetic effect mediated by beta-1 receptors.

questions.stem: A patient has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 65 mL. Calculate cardiac output in L/min.
questions.explanation: Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume: 80 x 65 = 5200 mL/min. Dividing by 1000 gives 5.2 L/min, which lies within the typical resting range of about 4 to 6 L/min.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has a cardiac output of 4.8 L/min at a heart rate of 96 beats per minute. Calculate the stroke volume in mL.
questions.explanation: Rearranging CO = HR x SV gives SV = CO / HR. Converting 4.8 L/min to 4800 mL/min and dividing by 96 beats per minute gives 50 mL. This is below a typical resting stroke volume of about 70 mL, so the patient maintains output by a high heart rate.

questions.stem: State the Frank-Starling relationship, explain the cellular basis for it, and give two reasons it is physiologically important.
markingGuide: Statement: within physiological limits, greater end-diastolic volume (preload) gives greater stroke volume
Basis: increased sarcomere stretch moves length towards optimal overlap and increases Ca2+ sensitivity of the contractile proteins
It is intrinsic to the myocardium and works without nerves or hormones
Importance 1: matches the outputs of the two ventricles in series
Importance 2: adjusts stroke volume beat by beat to changes in venous return
questions.explanation: A larger end-diastolic volume stretches sarcomeres and increases Ca2+ sensitivity, so the following contraction is stronger and the stroke volume is greater. Because this is intrinsic, it matches the output of the two ventricles and immediately adapts stroke volume to changes in venous return.

questions.stem: Compare the effects of sympathetic and parasympathetic stimulation on heart rate, atrioventricular conduction and ventricular contractility, naming the receptors and second messenger changes involved.
markingGuide: Sympathetic: noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors raises cAMP and PKA activity
Sympathetic: increases heart rate (steeper pacemaker potential), speeds AV conduction and increases contractility via more Ca2+ entry
Parasympathetic: acetylcholine on M2 receptors lowers cAMP and opens K+ channels
Parasympathetic: decreases heart rate and slows AV conduction
Parasympathetic has little direct effect on ventricular contractility because of sparse innervation
Resting vagal tone dominates, keeping resting rate below intrinsic SA rate (about 100 per minute)
questions.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation acts through beta-1 receptors and cAMP to raise heart rate, speed AV conduction and raise contractility. Parasympathetic stimulation acts through M2 receptors, lowering cAMP and opening K+ channels, which slows the nodes without much direct ventricular effect.

questions.stem: A heart transplant recipient has an intrinsic resting heart rate of about 100 beats per minute and, at the start of activity, his heart rate barely changes although his cardiac output rises. Explain both observations using cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume, the Frank-Starling relationship, and autonomic control.
markingGuide: Intrinsic SA node rate is about 100 beats per minute; in a normal heart vagal tone brakes this at rest
Transplanted heart is denervated, so there is no vagal braking at rest and no immediate sympathetic acceleration
Heart rate rises only slowly later because of circulating adrenaline acting on beta-1 receptors
Cardiac output rises early through stroke volume: increased venous return raises EDV
Frank-Starling: greater stretch gives stronger contraction and greater stroke volume without nerves
Uses CO = HR x SV to show a rise in SV at constant HR raises CO
questions.explanation: Without a nerve supply there is no vagal tone to slow the intrinsic SA rate, so rest rate is near 100 per minute, and there is no rapid sympathetic acceleration at the start of activity. Venous return, however, raises end-diastolic volume, and by the Frank-Starling relationship stroke volume rises, so CO = HR x SV rises even though heart rate is almost unchanged.
